messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: confusion on categorical distribution
parts: Hi, I was confused. In the description of the categorical distribution (model, page 278, it says that theta is a simplex. But in the example on page 29-30, theta is a vector that just happens to sum to 1 (that is, it’s not a “simplex” variable type). I ask because I’m using the categorical distribution but was struggling to get its input into a “simplex” form. So I think we need to fix the description of the categorical distribution in the model to make clear that it does not require a simplex variable type.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] confusion on categorical distribution [explanation of expression type system]
parts:
Short Answer:

The types of expressions, function arguments, and right-hand
sides of assignments do not involve constraints.

This is just a general feature of the language, and nothing to
do with the categorical distribution. It's discussed at length
in the manual, but I'd like to make it clearer for you and everyone
else if it's confusing.

Long Answer (with embedded Stan syntax tutorial presented computer
science style):

An EXPRESSION is something that has a value, like "1.2" or
"log(x)" or "x[i] * beta".

A STATEMENT is something that can be executed, like an assignment
statement or a log-prob increment statement. Statements can
be primitive, as in a simple assignment statement "x <- 3;" or they
can be made up of other statements, as in
"for (n in 1:N) y[n] ~ normal(mu,sigma)".

Each expression in Stan has a unique type that does not change as
the program is run --- that is, Stan is STATICALLY TYPED (compile time)
rather than DYNAMICALLY TYPED (run time).

Now here's the key to your question.

STAN'S EXPRESSION TYPES DO NOT INVOLVE CONSTRAINTS

An expression type can be a basic type:

primitive: int, real

matrix: matrix, vector, row_vector

or it can be an array type built out of another expression
type,

array: T[], where T is any expression type

Note that the way I wrote these without sizes is not accidental,
because as well as not involving constraints,

EXPRESSION TYPES DO NOT INVOLVE SIZES.

That is, if I declare a variable as matrix[M,N], the sizes M and N are
not part of the expression type. Sizes are determined only after data
is read in. For example, the data can determine the value of M and N
in the matrix declaration above.

Now here's how the type of an expression is calculated.

The types of LITERALS, such as "1" and "10.378e-3" are
determined by whether they have a period or "e" or not ("13"
is an int, whereas "1e-3" and "1.3" are real).

The types of VARIABLES are determined by their DECLARATIONS,
but IGNORING CONSTRAINTS AND SIZES. For example, a variable declared
as "real mu;" has the expression type real, as does
a variable declared as "real<lower=0> sigma;". An array
declared as "real x[N];" has type real[]. The fact that it
is an array is part of its type.
A variable declared with "matrix[M,N] A;" has type matrix,
as does a variable declared as "cov_matrix[K] Sigma;".

The types of other expressions, such as those built
from functions, "exp(sigma_raw)", arithmetic operators ("2 * beta"),
or indexing ("x[i]"), are determined by the rules of the language
(more on that below).

Each function specifies what is known as a SIGNATURE, which
is the type of its arguments and the type of its result. Some
functions are OVERLOADED so that they have more than one signature.
For example, the exp() function has four signatures in Stan:

real exp(real);
vector exp(vector);
row_vector exp(row_vector);
real[] exp(row_vector[]);

The signatures for each function are listed in the index.
This allows us to validate argument types at compile time and
also determine what the type of any function application is (it
is illegal to have two functions with the same argument types
and different result types).

Stan is not like BUGS, which I believe restricts some arguments
to be variables rather than general expressions (I don't think
JAGS has this restriction anywhere). In Stan, the argument
to a function or the right-hand side of an assignment can always
be any expression of the appropriate expression type. The function
will validate that its argument is appropriate and essentially
return -infinity and print a warning message if its fed an argument whose value
violates the requirements on function arguments (technically it's
raising an exception at the C++ which is caught by an optimizer
or sampler).

Constraints are used for only two purposes:

1. Defining the transform (and associated Jacobian) from
the constrained parameter to unconstrained.

2. Providing error checking and validation.
a. As each data variable is read in, its constraint is validated.
b. At the end of the transformed data, transformed parameters and
generated quantities block, the constraint is validated for
each variable declared in that block.

One of the reasons for this design is to allow intermediate
values for constrained types that do not satisfy the constraint.
As in:

cov_matrix[K] Sigma; // at this point, no value at all
for (m in 1:K)
for (n in 1:K)
Sigma[m,n] <- sigma[m] * sigma[n] * Omega[m,n];

During the loop, Sigma does not remain symmetric and positive definite.
That's why we only validate constraints at the end of blocks.

Sooooo, how do you think I should try to make this all clearer? It's
explained in pretty much the above terms in the section on
expressions and assignment and functions in the language reference
for the manual.

A big issue in refactoring the manual, which we want to do soon,
is pulling more of these descriptions of how the language works out
of the language reference section and describing them with less
technical language and lots of examples.

One issue I see is that most probability functions we have require
a constrained argument, even normal(mu,sigma), which requires
a sigma with a lower bound of 0. Nothing anywhere in Stan requires
an argument to a function (or the right-hand side of an assignment)
to be a variable of constrained type.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] confusion on categorical distribution [explanation of expression type system]
parts:
It's really simple!

Most programming languages work this way, so there
are only a few details that differentiate Stan from
say, C++, in terms of how types work.

One thing I didn't go into was promotion, which lets
you assign an int to a real. I'd like to make this fully
covariant for containers. What that means is that if you can
assign the elements of one container to the elements of the other,
then you can assign the container. That would let you everywhere
assign an int array to a real array, use an int array as an
argument to normal, and so on. And similarly for argument
passing, because argument passing is really just a kind of
assignment.

- Bob

>>> cov_matrix[K] Sigma; // at this point, no value at all
>>> for (m in 1:K)
>>> for (n in 1:K)
>>> Sigma[m,n] <- sigma[m] * sigma[n] * Omega[m,n];
>>>
>>> During the loop, Sigma does not remain symmetric and positive definite.
>>> That's why we only validate constraints at the end of blocks.
>>>
>>> Sooooo, how do you think I should try to make this all clearer? It's
>>> explained in pretty much the above terms in the section on
>>> expressions and assignment and functions in the language reference
>>> for the manual.
>>>
>>> A big issue in refactoring the manual, which we want to do soon,

>>>

>>>
>>> - Bob

>>> On Jul 12, 2014, at 6:40 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>>>
>>>> Short Answer:
>>>>
>>>> The types of expressions, function arguments, and right-hand
>>>> sides of assignments do not involve constraints.
>>>>
>>>> This is just a general feature of the language, and nothing to
>>>> do with the categorical distribution. It's discussed at length
>>>> in the manual, but I'd like to make it clearer for you and everyone
>>>> else if it's confusing.
>>>>
>>>> Long Answer (with embedded Stan syntax tutorial presented computer
>>>> science style):
>>>>
>>>> An EXPRESSION is something that has a value, like "1.2" or
>>>> "log(x)" or "x[i] * beta".
>>>>
>>>> A STATEMENT is something that can be executed, like an assignment
>>>> statement or a log-prob increment statement. Statements can
>>>> be primitive, as in a simple assignment statement "x <- 3;" or they
>>>> can be made up of other statements, as in
>>>> "for (n in 1:N) y[n] ~ normal(mu,sigma)".
>>>>
>>>> Each expression in Stan has a unique type that does not change as
>>>> the program is run --- that is, Stan is STATICALLY TYPED (compile time)
>>>> rather than DYNAMICALLY TYPED (run time).
>>>>
>>>> Now here's the key to your question.
>>>>
>>>> STAN'S EXPRESSION TYPES DO NOT INVOLVE CONSTRAINTS
>>>>
>>>> An expression type can be a basic type:
>>>>
>>>> primitive: int, real
>>>>
>>>> matrix: matrix, vector, row_vector
>>>>
>>>> or it can be an array type built out of another expression
>>>> type,
>>>>
>>>> array: T[], where T is any expression type
>>>>
>>>> Note that the way I wrote these without sizes is not accidental,
>>>> because as well as not involving constraints,
>>>>
>>>> EXPRESSION TYPES DO NOT INVOLVE SIZES.
>>>>
>>>> That is, if I declare a variable as matrix[M,N], the sizes M and N are
>>>> not part of the expression type. Sizes are determined only after data
>>>> is read in. For example, the data can determine the value of M and N
>>>> in the matrix declaration above.
>>>>
>>>> Now here's how the type of an expression is calculated.
>>>>
>>>> The types of LITERALS, such as "1" and "10.378e-3" are
>>>> determined by whether they have a period or "e" or not ("13"
>>>> is an int, whereas "1e-3" and "1.3" are real).
>>>>
>>>> The types of VARIABLES are determined by their DECLARATIONS,
>>>> but IGNORING CONSTRAINTS AND SIZES. For example, a variable declared
>>>> as "real mu;" has the expression type real, as does
>>>> a variable declared as "real<lower=0> sigma;". An array
>>>> declared as "real x[N];" has type real[]. The fact that it
>>>> is an array is part of its type.
>>>> A variable declared with "matrix[M,N] A;" has type matrix,
>>>> as does a variable declared as "cov_matrix[K] Sigma;".
>>>>
>>>> The types of other expressions, such as those built
>>>> from functions, "exp(sigma_raw)", arithmetic operators ("2 * beta"),
>>>> or indexing ("x[i]"), are determined by the rules of the language
>>>> (more on that below).
>>>>
>>>> Each function specifies what is known as a SIGNATURE, which
>>>> is the type of its arguments and the type of its result. Some
>>>> functions are OVERLOADED so that they have more than one signature.
>>>> For example, the exp() function has four signatures in Stan:
>>>>
>>>> real exp(real);
>>>> vector exp(vector);
>>>> row_vector exp(row_vector);
>>>> real[] exp(row_vector[]);
>>>>
>>>> The signatures for each function are listed in the index.
>>>> This allows us to validate argument types at compile time and
>>>> also determine what the type of any function application is (it
>>>> is illegal to have two functions with the same argument types
>>>> and different result types).
>>>>
>>>> Stan is not like BUGS, which I believe restricts some arguments
>>>> to be variables rather than general expressions (I don't think
>>>> JAGS has this restriction anywhere). In Stan, the argument
>>>> to a function or the right-hand side of an assignment can always
>>>> be any expression of the appropriate expression type. The function
>>>> will validate that its argument is appropriate and essentially
>>>> return -infinity and print a warning message if its fed an argument whose value
>>>> violates the requirements on function arguments (technically it's
>>>> raising an exception at the C++ which is caught by an optimizer
>>>> or sampler).
>>>>
>>>> Constraints are used for only two purposes:
>>>>
>>>> 1. Defining the transform (and associated Jacobian) from
>>>> the constrained parameter to unconstrained.
>>>>
>>>> 2. Providing error checking and validation.
>>>> a. As each data variable is read in, its constraint is validated.
>>>> b. At the end of the transformed data, transformed parameters and
>>>> generated quantities block, the constraint is validated for
>>>> each variable declared in that block.
>>>>
>>>> One of the reasons for this design is to allow intermediate
>>>> values for constrained types that do not satisfy the constraint.
>>>> As in:
>>>>
>>>> cov_matrix[K] Sigma; // at this point, no value at all
>>>> for (m in 1:K)
>>>> for (n in 1:K)
>>>> Sigma[m,n] <- sigma[m] * sigma[n] * Omega[m,n];
>>>>
>>>> During the loop, Sigma does not remain symmetric and positive definite.
>>>> That's why we only validate constraints at the end of blocks.
>>>>
>>>> Sooooo, how do you think I should try to make this all clearer? It's
>>>> explained in pretty much the above terms in the section on
>>>> expressions and assignment and functions in the language reference
>>>> for the manual.
>>>>
>>>> A big issue in refactoring the manual, which we want to do soon,
>>>> is pulling more of these descriptions of how the language works out
>>>> of the language reference section and describing them with less
>>>> technical language and lots of examples.
>>>>
>>>> One issue I see is that most probability functions we have require
>>>> a constrained argument, even normal(mu,sigma), which requires
>>>> a sigma with a lower bound of 0. Nothing anywhere in Stan requires
>>>> an argument to a function (or the right-hand side of an assignment)
>>>> to be a variable of constrained type.
>>>>
>>>> - Bob
